deep_dive.title: MM-Net: A Multimodal Multi-Task Network for Sleep Staging and Sleep Apnea Assessment After Ischemic Stroke
deep_dive.abstract: Automated polysomnography after ischemic stroke is challenging because of altered sleep-related neural activity and concurrent respiratory disturbances. Existing stroke-specific approaches mainly address sleep-stage classification, leaving joint analysis of sleep architecture and respiratory events underexplored. Moreover, adapting pretrained EEG encoders introduces a representation inconsistency when downstream models are trained on embeddings from previously seen patients but evaluated on unseen individuals. We propose MM-Net, a multimodal multi-task framework that resolves this inconsistency through cross-fitting and ridge-based embedding alignment. Sleep-adapted EEG-EOG representations and engineered neural descriptors are fused with learned cardiorespiratory features through cross-attention and shared temporal modeling for simultaneous sleep staging and respiratory-event detection. On iSLEEPS (99 patients with subacute ischemic stroke), ten-fold patient-independent evaluation achieved 76.3% staging accuracy (Cohen's $κ$ = 0.656) and 0.825 respiratory-event AUC, outperforming the evaluated baselines under matched protocols. The sleep-adapted encoder improved the downstream model when its embeddings were aligned, raising staging accuracy by 1.4 percentage points over the frozen encoder ($p$ = 0.020) versus 0.2 points without alignment. MM-Net also achieved 86.4% staging accuracy on Sleep-EDF, above every single-EEG architecture reimplemented on the same recordings, and 80.3% staging accuracy with 0.889 respiratory AUC on ISRUC-I, exceeding its retrained staging baselines. Without retraining, the iSLEEPS-trained model retained respiratory AUCs of 0.833 on ISRUC-I and 0.841 on UCD. These findings support representation-consistent neural adaptation and joint physiological modeling across stroke, healthy-sleep, and sleep-disorder cohorts.

quick_skim.title: Neuronal Identity as an Organizational Basis for Analyzing Neural Population Dynamics
quick_skim.abstract: Individual neurons exhibit diverse molecular, morphological, and electrophysiological properties that shape their distinct roles in neural circuits. While these multimodal features are largely shared across individuals, they remain an underutilized source of information in analyzing neural population dynamics. We posit that these shared biological profiles provide a common reference for relating neural dynamics across subjects and recording sessions. Our framework leverages this structure by routing neurons into latent groups based on their biological profiles and analyzing population dynamics through group-level representations. Because these assignments are anchored in biological properties that are consistent across subjects, the learned organization supports transfer to unseen animals without retraining or neuron-wise correspondence. We evaluate our framework on whole-brain calcium imaging in larval zebrafish and large-scale electrophysiology in the mouse visual cortex. Across both species and recording modalities, the framework delivers state-of-the-art performance in both neural decoding and manifold analysis: it achieves superior decoding of behavior and stimulus labels while better preserving the temporal consistency and local geometric structure of latent trajectories on unseen data. Our experiments demonstrate that not only does providing biological features improve baseline performance, but our proposed framework achieves even stronger results by using these properties to explicitly structure the population rather than treating them as auxiliary inputs. Together, these results suggest that organizing neural populations by their multimodal biological features offers a promising framework for generalizing population dynamics across subjects and recording sessions.

quick_skim.title: Cross-User Adaptation for sEMG Gesture Recognition via Continual Learning
quick_skim.abstract: Prosthetic and assistive interfaces increasingly depend on decoding hand gestures from surface electromyography (sEMG). Because the signal is shaped by person-specific factors, the recurrent neural networks (RNNs) commonly used to model these temporal streams must adapt to new wearers and new gesture classes after deployment. Continual learning (CL) enables this adaptation without retraining from scratch, yet applying it to recurrent sEMG models is not straightforward. Standard recurrent training practices can destabilize learning, and which CL strategy holds up under realistic cross-user drift is unestablished. We evaluate three representative CL strategies under domain- and class-incremental drift on NinaPro DB1, and find experience replay to outperform elastic weight consolidation (EWC) and naive fine-tuning. It reaches 83.3% final accuracy for class-incremental drift while limiting forgetting to 1.8-5.8% accuracy drop, as against 16.2-28.5% for EWC and naive training. We further show these models must be trained on shuffled, independently-windowed segments. Streaming windows in temporal order collapses the network into predicting a single dominant gesture, while a shuffled, stateless regime trains stably. Finally, hand-crafted time-domain features raise per-task accuracy by up to about 40% over raw signals, but only replay preserves that gain under class-incremental drift.

quick_skim.title: Comparing Temporal Deep Learning Architectures for Discrete Cross-User Myoelectric Control
quick_skim.abstract: The recognition of dynamic gestures via discrete myoelectric control is becoming an attractive input modality for event-based human-machine interaction. While recent work suggests that discrete cross-user models are possible (i.e., no calibration data is required from the end user), few have evaluated techniques to optimize these systems and their generalizability to new randomly prompted data simulating real-world discrete control is relatively unknown. Using the 612-user EMG-EPN dataset, this work benchmarks five temporal deep-learning approaches, evaluates the tradeoff between performance and model complexity, and compares hand-crafted and machine-learned feature extraction techniques. The CNN-GRU achieved the best accuracy of 93% when tested on 184 previously unseen users. These models were then evaluated on a different, more realistic, unsegmented dataset, wherein users were randomly prompted to elicit discrete gestures during a continuous data collection. This dataset was recorded five years apart and in a separate country from the data used to train the original model. Results show that the cross-user results scale to this new dataset (accuracies of 96%) even though no feedback was given to users during the elicitation of gestures. These findings highlight the exciting potential of discrete zero-shot cross-user myoelectric control and offer valuable insights for the continued advancement of this promising technology.

quick_skim.title: Revisiting entropy and entropy-related magnitudes of a symbolic sequence and their estimation
quick_skim.abstract: This article revisits entropy and related magnitudes (entropy density, effective measure complexity, and informational distance) for the analysis of sequential data. We present their mathematical foundations within information theory and ergodic theory, establishing connections between probabilistic Shannon entropy and algorithmic Kolmogorov complexity. A central result, Zivs theorem, demonstrates the asymptotic equivalence between the normalised number of distinct words and entropy density, providing the theoretical basis for estimation via Lempel-Ziv factorisation. We examine the convergence properties of these magnitudes and introduce estimation procedures for finite sequences, including a method for the effective measure complexity and the transfer entropy rate. An open-source software library implementing parallel algorithms for efficient Lempel-Ziv factorisation is presented. The practical utility of the framework is illustrated through three case studies: functional brain connectivity analysis from fMRI data, characterisation of spatiotemporal dynamics in coupled nonlinear oscillators, and electrocardiogram-based classification of atrial fibrillation, demonstrating how entropic measures capture meaningful structural and dynamical properties across diverse domains.

quick_skim.title: LUCID: Local Understanding of Covariate Importance with Conditional Density Estimation
quick_skim.abstract: Computing local-level variable importance (VI) is critical for understanding machine learning models. Local permutation-based VI metrics offer a simple yet powerful approach, measuring how much a model's output changes when perturbing its inputs. However, existing perturbation strategies often ignore feature dependence or account for it only through restricted approximations. Perturbing a feature without fully respecting this dependence can generate unrealistic counterfactuals, thereby evaluating the model in regions unsupported by the observed data distribution. We address this gap by introducing a new model-agnostic local VI metric and estimator, Local Understanding of Covariate Importance with conditional Density estimation (LUCID). LUCID perturbs features of interest using plausible values drawn from the full conditional distribution given the remaining observed features. We establish theoretical connections between LUCID and existing VI measures, and provide an estimator with convergence guarantees and uncertainty quantification. Finally, we demonstrate LUCID's stable performance and practical utility across simulated and real-world examples.

quick_skim.title: Physiology-Informed Audio Quality and Listening Effort Estimation
quick_skim.abstract: Audio systems aim to maximise the listener's perceived quality, traditionally evaluated through mean opinion scoring (MOS), a subjective process that is slow, costly, and collected only after playback. Machine learning now predicts MOS directly from the audio, but in generalising across participants it tends to discard the subject variance that defines individual perception. Neurophysiological measures may offer a complementary signal taken directly from the listener, objective, implicit, and continuous, though prior work has relied on laboratory-grade EEG and fNIRS. We ask how practical consumer-grade devices compare, and whether they might recover population-level audio-quality trends and, when calibrated per listener, track that listener's effort. Recording 32-channel laboratory EEG alongside wearable EEG, fNIRS, and eye tracking from thirty listeners, our results suggest commercial wearable and optical sensing can decode audio quality at statistically significant levels and recover listening effort per listener. These findings may point towards platforms tuned not only to perceived quality but to the effort a clip demands, read from the listener's own response as they listen.
